---
url: /cuora/tutorials/first-secret.md
---
# Your first secret

A full cuora lifecycle — bootstrap, seal, declare, inject, audit —
in a throwaway `HOME` so nothing touches your real config. All
values below are fake.

## Setup

```sh
export HOME="$(mktemp -d)"        # scratch HOME for this tutorial
export XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$HOME/.config"
export XDG_DATA_HOME="$HOME/.local/share"
export CUORA_IDENTITY_BACKEND=file  # keyring is per-session, not
                                  # per-HOME — opt into the keyfile
                                  # so nothing touches your real store

cuora init
```

```text
identity: /tmp/tmp.…/.config/cuora/identity.txt (generated)
recipient: age1…
vault:     /tmp/tmp.…/.local/share/cuora/vault.age
```

On stderr you'll also see the first audit event — every cuora op
emits one ndjson line there:

```json
{"ts":"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z","actor":"you","op":"init","env":"dev","outcome":"ok"}
```

## Seal a value

```sh
printf '%s' 'sk_test_FAKE000000000000000000' | cuora put cuora://billing/stripe
```

```text
stored cuora://billing/stripe (v1)
```

The plaintext went in on stdin — never an argument. What's on
disk is age ciphertext:

```sh
file "$XDG_DATA_HOME/cuora/vault.age"   # data — not readable
```

## Declare and inject

```sh
cat > cuora.toml <<'EOF'
[secrets]
STRIPE_KEY = "cuora://billing/stripe"
EOF

cuora run -- 'echo "key starts with: ${STRIPE_KEY:0:7}…"'
```

```text
key starts with: sk_test…
```

The child saw `$STRIPE_KEY` as a normal env var; nothing else —
not your shell, not a file — ever held it. And the audit wire
recorded the materialization:

```json
{"ts":"…","actor":"you","op":"run","rref":"billing/stripe","env":"dev","outcome":"ok"}
```

## List without spilling

```sh
cuora list
# cuora://billing/stripe

cuora list --json
# [{"ref":"cuora://billing/stripe","env":"dev","version":1,"created_at":"…","rotated_at":null}]
```

`list` is names plus metadata — never values. The only surfaces
that print a value are `get` (the escape hatch) and `env`
(exports for `eval`).

## Rotate and verify

```sh
printf '%s' 'sk_test_FAKE111111111111111111' | cuora rotate cuora://billing/stripe
# rotated cuora://billing/stripe (v2)

cuora check
# config: /tmp/tmp.…/cuora.toml
# env: dev → vault "local"
# vault "local" (age): readable
# secret STRIPE_KEY → cuora://billing/stripe (env dev): resolves
# ok
```

`rotate` requires the ref to exist (it's deliberate rotation,
not upsert), bumps the version, and stamps `rotated_at`.

## Clean up

```sh
rm -rf "$HOME"      # the scratch vault and identity go with it
```

## Where next

* [Add a secret](../how-to/add-a-secret.md) — multi-env and
  pinning.
* [Route envs to vaults](../how-to/route-envs-to-vaults.md) —
  `prod` to a remote vault.
* [The audit wire](../reference/audit-events.md) — the ndjson
  contract.

---

---
url: /cuora/how-to/add-a-secret.md
---
# Add a secret

Store a value under an `cuora://` ref in the vault backing an env.

## The pipe path (scripts and agents)

```sh
printf '%s' "$VALUE" | cuora put cuora://ns/name
```

* stdin is read to EOF; **one** trailing newline is stripped, the
  rest is verbatim (multi-line values work).
* Empty input fails — you can't store a blank secret.
* The value is never an argument: args land in shell history and
  `/proc`.

Other sources that already hold the value pipe the same way:

```sh
pass show stripe/test | cuora put cuora://billing/stripe
op read "op://vault/stripe/test" | cuora put cuora://billing/stripe --env dev
```

## The interactive path (humans)

```sh
cuora put cuora://ns/name          # stdin is a tty → hidden /dev/tty prompt
```

The prompt doesn't echo — paste the value, hit enter.

## Pick the env

Env is resolution *context*, not part of the name — the same
`cuora://ns/name` ref can hold different values per env:

```sh
printf dev-token   | cuora put cuora://billing/stripe --env dev
printf prod-token  | cuora put cuora://prod/billing/stripe   # env pin
```

`cuora://prod/…` pins the env regardless of `--env`/`CUORA_ENV`;
the bare form resolves under the selected env.

## Upsert semantics

`put` is an upsert: a new ref starts at `version = 1`; re-putting
an existing ref replaces the value and bumps the version but is
*not* a rotation (`rotated_at` stays untouched — use
[`cuora rotate`](rotate-a-secret.md) for deliberate rotations).

## Remove

```sh
cuora rm cuora://ns/name
```

## Verify

```sh
cuora list [--env prod]      # refs only — never values
cuora check                  # declared [secrets] entries resolve?
```

---

---
url: /cuora/how-to/inject-into-a-process.md
---
# Inject secrets into a process

`cuora run` is the agent path — resolved values become env vars in
the child and nowhere else. `cuora env` is the human path — export
lines for `eval`.

## Declare the surface

`[secrets]` in `cuora.toml` bounds what `run`/`env` may inject:

```toml
[secrets]
STRIPE_KEY   = "cuora://billing/stripe"
DATABASE_URL = "cuora://prod/db/url"     # env pin: prod, always
```

Nothing outside this table (plus `-s` ad-hoc pairs) is injectable
— least privilege, and `cuora check` verifies every entry resolves.

## `cuora run` — two exec modes

```sh
# one arg → bash -c — pipes, redirects, $VAR expansion
cuora run -- 'psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "select 1" | tee out.log'

# several args → argv[0] exec'd directly, NO shell —
# the program reads its own environment
cuora run -- stripe charges list --limit 3
```

Prefer argv mode when the command has arguments — no quoting
puzzles. One caveat: with no shell in the child there is no
`$VAR` expansion — write `$STRIPE_KEY` in argv and *your* outer
shell eats it (to an empty string) before cuora runs. Use `bash
-c` mode when the command line itself needs the value.

Exit code is the child's; a child's non-zero exit is not an cuora
failure (no `error` audit event).

## Ad-hoc pairs: `-s VAR=cuora://ref`

Repeatable, merged over `[secrets]` (same `VAR` — the `-s` pair
wins):

```sh
cuora run -s TEMP_TOKEN=cuora://ci/token -- ./deploy.sh
```

## Missing secrets fail closed

If any declared or `-s` ref isn't stored in its env, `run` fails
before spawning — partial injection is worse than none.

## `cuora env` — the human path

```sh
eval "$(cuora env)"                              # export every declared VAR
eval "$(cuora env -s EXTRA=cuora://misc/extra)"   # plus ad-hoc pairs
cuora env --json                                 # {"VAR": "value"} map
```

Output is `export VAR='…'` with shell-safe quoting for any value.
This prints plaintext into your shell environment — that's why
it's the *human* path: agents should `run` instead. A
`[guardrails]` deny on `env` is the owner's hint.

## The audit trail

Each resolved ref emits one materialization event on stderr —
`op` is `run` or `env`, `rref` the ref path, `outcome: "ok"`. See
[the audit wire](../reference/audit-events.md).

---

---
url: /cuora/how-to/rotate-a-secret.md
---
# Rotate a secret

Replace a stored value deliberately — version bump plus a
`rotated_at` timestamp, and an audit event.

```sh
printf '%s' "$NEW_VALUE" | cuora rotate cuora://billing/stripe
# rotated cuora://billing/stripe (v3)
```

Like `put`, the value arrives on stdin (or a hidden `/dev/tty`
prompt) — never an argument.

## `rotate` vs re-`put`

| | `put` (upsert) | `rotate` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Missing ref | creates it (v1) | **fails** — `NotFound` |
| `version` | +1 | +1 |
| `rotated_at` | untouched | stamped |

Rotation is intentional: a missing ref failing loudly catches a
typo'd ref or wrong env that `put` would silently create.

## Rotate in a specific env

```sh
printf '%s' "$PROD_VALUE" | cuora rotate cuora://prod/billing/stripe
# or: --env prod
```

## Verify

```sh
cuora list --json --env prod
# … "version": 3, "rotated_at": "2026-…"
```

Downstream consumers pick the new value up on their next
`cuora run` — resolution happens at exec time, nothing caches it.

If the value was pushed to a deploy sink, re-push it:
[`cuora deploy cuora://billing/stripe`](deploy-to-a-sink.md) — the
sink is write-only and doesn't follow the vault on its own.

---

---
url: /cuora/how-to/route-envs-to-vaults.md
---
# Route envs to vaults

Envs are the routing axis: `[envs]` maps each env name to a
`[vaults]` backend, so `dev` can stay on the local age file while
`prod` reads from a remote ciphertext store.

## The tables

```toml
[vaults.local]                 # the built-in default — entry optional
kind = "age"
# path / identity / recipients  # optional overrides

[vaults.cloud]
kind = "cf"                    # self-hosted Worker + D1, age ciphertext
url = "https://cuora-vault.you.workers.dev"
token_env = "CUORA_CF_TOKEN"    # env var NAME — token value stays in env

[envs]
dev = "local"                  # bare-name form
prod = { vault = "cloud" }     # table form
```

Rules:

* `local` always exists implicitly (age, default paths) — a
  `[vaults.local]` entry only overrides it.
* Envs not listed route to `local`. `dev`/`staging`/`prod` always
  exist; `[envs]` keys add custom envs (`ci`, `qa`, …).
* `token_env` names the env var carrying the credential — the
  *name* is in config, the *value* only in the process env.
* `CUORA_IDENTITY_FILE` overrides the age identity path globally.

## What changes at run time

```sh
cuora list --env prod          # opens the "cloud" vault over HTTPS
cuora put cuora://prod/x/y      # pin → writes to "cloud"
cuora run --env prod -- ./app  # [secrets] resolve under prod → cloud
```

The ref spelling doesn't change — `cuora://ns/name` is env-agnostic;
routing decides which backend serves it.

## The `cf` backend

`kind = "cf"` talks to your own Cloudflare Worker fronting D1.
All encryption is client-side: the worker stores opaque age
ciphertext and has no key material. Setup is a how-to of its own —
see [Cloudflare Worker setup](cloudflare-worker-setup.md).

## Verify routing

```sh
cuora check
# env: dev → vault "local"
# vault "local" (age): readable
# vault "cloud" (cf): readable      ← actually probed over the wire
```

`check` reports every configured and routed vault — including
ones no env currently routes to — and fails on routes pointing at
undeclared vault names.

---

---
url: /cuora/how-to/cached-vaults.md
---
# Cache a remote vault locally

A remote vault (`kind = "cf"`) costs a network round-trip per
read and goes hard-down offline. `[vaults.*] cache` fronts it
with a read-through, age-encrypted local mirror — `get`/`list`
serve the cache while it's fresh, misses fetch remote and
write-through, and a remote failure falls back to the stale copy.

## Turn it on

```toml
[vaults.cloud]
kind = "cf"
url = "https://cuora-vault.you.workers.dev"
token_env = "CUORA_CF_TOKEN"
cache = ["dev"]              # cache only the dev env
# cache = true              # or: cache every env
# cache_ttl_secs = 600      # freshness window, default 300
```

Three scope forms — `true` for every env, `"dev"` for one,
`["dev", "staging"]` for a set. `cache = false` and `cache = []`
are the same as leaving it out.

## What lands on disk

Rows mirror into `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/cuora/<vault>.age` (else
`~/.cache/cuora/`) — an ordinary age vault encrypted to the same
identity and recipients as the vault itself, so the cache needs
no new key material and no new threat surface. Each cached row
carries the remote `version`/`rotated_at` verbatim plus a
`fetched_at` stamp; a tiny `cloud.listed.json` sidecar holds
per-env list markers (env names and timestamps, never refs or
values). It's a cache: delete the directory and it rebuilds.

## Freshness model

* **Within the TTL** a cached `get`/`list` answers with no
  network at all — a burst of `cuora run`s costs one round-trip.
* **Past the TTL** the read goes remote and rewrites the row.
* **Remote unreachable** — the stale copy answers. That's the
  offline mode the cache exists for, not an error.
* **Writes never serve stale**: `put`/`rotate`/`rm` always hit
  the remote first, then update or invalidate the mirror. A
  remote `rm` propagates into the cache on the next `list`.

The tradeoff to know: within the TTL another writer's change
isn't visible — the remote's own change is. Shorten
`cache_ttl_secs` if your env rotates often.

## Scope it — prod stays live

```toml
[envs]
dev = { vault = "cloud" }    # cached — fast, offline-capable
prod = { vault = "cloud" }   # out of scope → every read live-fetches
```

`cache = ["dev"]` means prod rows *never touch the disk mirror* —
every prod verb is a straight remote call. A stale prod secret
is a footgun; the scope is the safety rail.

## Verify

```sh
cuora get cuora://a/b       # first call: remote fetch + write-through
cuora get cuora://a/b       # second call: cache hit, no round-trip
ls ~/.cache/cuora/         # cloud.age + cloud.listed.json
cuora check                # probes the remote like before
```

A cache file that won't decrypt is moved aside to
`<vault>.corrupt` and rebuilt — corruption degrades to
remote-only reads, never to a wrong answer.

url: /cuora/how-to/deploy-to-a-sink.md
---
# Deploy a secret to a sink

`cuora deploy` pushes a vault-stored value to a write-only target —
a `[deploy.NAME]` table in `cuora.toml`. The vault is the source of
truth; the sink serves your runtimes directly (e.g. a Worker
reading a Secrets Store binding).

## Configure a target

```toml
[deploy.prod]
kind = "cf-secrets-store"      # Cloudflare account Secrets Store
account_id = "00000000000000000000000000000000"
store_id   = "00000000000000000000000000000000"
# token_env = "CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN"   # default; env var NAME only
```

The API token comes from the env var named by `token_env`
(default `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`) — never from the file.

## Push

```sh
cuora deploy cuora://billing/stripe --target prod
# deployed cuora://billing/stripe → "prod" as dev_billing_stripe (created)
```

* `--target` may be omitted when exactly one `[deploy.*]` table is
  configured; several targets make it required.
* The sink-side name is derived and stable —
  `env + ref-path` underscored (`dev_billing_stripe`).
* Re-deploying updates in place (`updated`, not `created`).

## The direction is one-way

Deploy targets are **sinks**, not sources: the plaintext crosses
to the sink exactly once, at push time, and nothing ever reads it
back through cuora. A deploy emits a `deploy` audit event for the
ref.

## Rotate → re-deploy

`cuora rotate` changes the vault; the sink doesn't follow on its
own. Re-push after rotation:

```sh
printf '%s' "$NEW_VALUE" | cuora rotate cuora://prod/billing/stripe
cuora deploy cuora://prod/billing/stripe --target prod
```

## Verify

`cuora check` validates deploy tables (kind known, `account_id` +
`store_id` present) as findings — it doesn't push anything.

url: /cuora/how-to/guardrails-for-agents.md
---
# Guardrails for agents

`[guardrails]` is an advisory op table — the owner declaring
"agents get these verbs, not those". It runs before the op
touches the vault, on every verb.

```toml
[guardrails]
deny = ["get", "env", "put", "rm", "rotate", "deploy"]
```

```toml
[guardrails]
default = "deny"               # unlisted ops refused
allow = ["run", "list", "check", "manifest", "schema"]
```

* `deny` wins over `allow`; `default` covers the rest
  (default `"allow"`).
* Op names match `cuora manifest`'s `ops` list:
  `init, put, get, list, rm, rotate, run, env, check, deploy,
  migrate, serve, manifest, schema`.
* `manifest`/`schema`/`gen-cli-docs` run before config load —
  introspection is never gated.

## What a denial looks like

```text
cuora: op 'get' denied by guardrails in ./cuora.toml
       (advisory — remove/relax the rule to allow)
```

…plus an `outcome: "denied"` audit event carrying the requested
ref. Exit is non-zero; `--json` emits `{"error": "…"}`.

## Honest scope: advisory, not policy

Guardrails are accident prevention, not enforcement:

* `CUORA_ACTOR` (and `--actor`) is self-claimed — attribution, not
  identity.
* Nothing stops a determined process from editing `cuora.toml` or
  running the binary differently. Real policy enforcement is
  peregrin's job (cuora's orchestrator neighbor); cuora's contract
  is to *honor* the declared rules and *record* every refusal.

If a guardrail denies your op as an agent: don't work around it.
Use an allowed verb (`run` instead of `get`), or surface the
denial to the human — it's the owner telling you the boundary.

## Typical agent posture

Deny every value-egress and mutation verb; allow the
inject-and-run path:

```toml
[guardrails]
default = "deny"
allow = ["run", "list", "check"]
```

The agent can `cuora run` (values materialize inside the child,
never in its context) and can list refs — but `get`/`env`, the
plaintext printers, are off.

---

url: /cuora/how-to/cloudflare-worker-setup.md
---
# Cloudflare Worker setup

The `cf` vault kind is two halves: `cuora-vault-cf` in the CLI
(client-side age encryption + blocking HTTP) and a Worker you
self-host — a thin store fronting D1 that holds **opaque
ciphertext only**. The worker has no key material and cannot read
what it serves.

## What you're deploying

The worker source, schema, and the authoritative deploy
walkthrough live in the repo:

* [`crates/cuora-vault-cf/worker/README.md`](https://github.com/9aia/cuora/blob/main/crates/cuora-vault-cf/worker/README.md)
  — wire protocol (`cuora-vault-cf/2`), `wrangler` steps
* `worker/index.js` — the Worker (constant-time auth, scoped
  tokens, CuoraHmac verification + REST verbs)
* `worker/schema.sql` — the D1 table (`name` column added in v2 —
  `ALTER TABLE secrets ADD COLUMN name TEXT` on an existing db)
* `worker/wrangler.toml` — binding config

The short version:

```sh
cd crates/cuora-vault-cf/worker
wrangler d1 create cuora-vault                  # → paste database_id into wrangler.toml
wrangler d1 execute cuora-vault --file=schema.sql
wrangler secret put CUORA_VAULT_TOKEN           # legacy single bearer, or:
wrangler secret put CUORA_VAULT_TOKENS          # scoped token map (JSON) — below
wrangler deploy
```

Then point a vault at it in `cuora.toml`:

```toml
[vaults.cloud]
kind = "cf"
url = "https://cuora-vault.you.workers.dev"
token_env = "CUORA_CF_TOKEN"

[envs]
prod = { vault = "cloud" }
```

and export the bearer token under the name `token_env` chose
(`export CUORA_CF_TOKEN=…`).

## Scoped tokens (wire v2)

One static bearer for every env is a big blast radius. Wire v2
scopes tokens per env: the worker reads `CUORA_VAULT_TOKENS`, a JSON
map of `token_id → {token, scopes}`, and enforces
`{env|"*" → {read, write}}` after auth — a leaked `dev` token can't
read `prod`.

```json
{
  "ops/cf-token-dev": {
    "token": "<dev-token-secret>",
    "scopes": { "dev": { "read": true, "write": true } }
  },
  "ops/cf-token-viewer": {
    "token": "<viewer-secret>",
    "scopes": { "*": { "read": true, "write": false } }
  }
}
```

On the client side, each scoped credential is an `cuora://` ref —
the token itself lives as a secret in the **`local` vault** under
the env it scopes; the ref path is the wire `token_id`:

```toml
[vaults.cloud.tokens]
dev = "cuora://ops/cf-token-dev"
prod = "cuora://ops/cf-token-prod"
```

```sh
printf '%s' '<dev-token-secret>' | cuora put cuora://ops/cf-token-dev --env dev
printf '%s' '<prod-token-secret>' | cuora put cuora://ops/cf-token-prod --env prod
```

With a scoped token configured the client signs every request —
`Authorization: CuoraHmac &lt;token_id&gt;, &lt;ts&gt;, &lt;sig&gt;` where
`sig = hex HMAC-SHA256(token, method+path+ts+sha256(body))` and `ts`
must be within the worker's 60-second replay window. **The token
never travels.** `Bearer` stays accepted during migration, so a
mixed fleet upgrades gracefully.

**Rotation is `wrangler secret put`** — replace the value inside
`CUORA_VAULT_TOKENS`, then `cuora put` the new secret at the token
ref. There is deliberately no admin route.

## Private refs (opt-in)

By default `ref` and `env` are visible to the store — values are
ciphertext, but *which secrets exist* is metadata. With
`private_refs = true` the client derives
`ref_key = HMAC(identity-derived-key, env + "/" + ref)` and uses it
as the storage key; each record also carries a `name` blob — age
ciphertext of the real ref — so `list` maps keys back while the
store sees only hex:

```toml
[vaults.cloud]
kind = "cf"
url = "…"
private_refs = true
```

Existing rows aren't rewritten by the flag alone — run:

```sh
cuora migrate --private-refs
```

which re-keys every plaintext-named row (ciphertext moves verbatim,
old keys deleted after new ones land). A vault mixing plain and
private rows is **mixed-mode**: `list`/`check` fail closed until
you migrate — deliberately, since reading the wrong interpretation
silently is worse than failing. Turning `private_refs` off again on
a private vault fails closed the other way; migrating back is a
manual re-put.

## Client-side crypto boundary

`put` seals the value with age **before** it leaves the machine;
`get` unseals after it arrives. The wire — and the D1 row —
carries `{"ciphertext", "name", "version", created_at, rotated_at}`.
A compromised worker yields ciphertext and, at most, opaque keys —
not values, not ref names (with `private_refs`). Your local
`identity.txt` is the only key, same file the local age vault uses;
the private-refs derivation is keyed by it, so rotating the
identity means a full re-key + migrate.

## Verify

```sh
cuora check --env prod
# vault "cloud" (cf): readable     ← probes the worker over HTTPS
```

An unreachable worker or a bad token shows up as a finding —
`check` fails open in the report, never panics.

## Deploy sinks vs the vault

Don't confuse the two CF surfaces:

* `[vaults.cloud] kind = "cf"` — a *readable* ciphertext store
  (your Worker + D1). Source of truth.
* `[deploy.prod] kind = "cf-secrets-store"` — a *write-only*
  Cloudflare Secrets Store sink `cuora deploy` pushes plaintext
  into for Workers to consume via bindings. See
  [deploy to a sink](deploy-to-a-sink.md).

# Command-Line Help for `cuora`

This document contains the help content for the `cuora` command-line program.

**Command Overview:**

* [`cuora`↴](#cuora)
* [`cuora init`↴](#cuora-init)
* [`cuora put`↴](#cuora-put)
* [`cuora get`↴](#cuora-get)
* [`cuora list`↴](#cuora-list)
* [`cuora rm`↴](#cuora-rm)
* [`cuora rotate`↴](#cuora-rotate)
* [`cuora run`↴](#cuora-run)
* [`cuora env`↴](#cuora-env)
* [`cuora check`↴](#cuora-check)
* [`cuora migrate`↴](#cuora-migrate)
* [`cuora deploy`↴](#cuora-deploy)
* [`cuora serve`↴](#cuora-serve)
* [`cuora manifest`↴](#cuora-manifest)
* [`cuora schema`↴](#cuora-schema)

## `cuora`

cuora — secrets broker for agents: `cuora://` refs, redaction, env-injection instead of plaintext.

Refs name logical secrets (`cuora://billing/stripe`); `--env` picks the resolution context. `[secrets]` in cuora.toml bounds what `run`/`env` may inject. `manifest`/`schema` describe the surface for machines; every verb honors `--json`.

**Usage:** `cuora [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>`

###### **Subcommands:**

* `init` — Bootstrap: store the age identity in the system keyring when a session secret store is reachable — importing an existing identity.txt rather than orphaning it — else the `~/.config/cuora/identity.txt` keyfile (0600). Verifies the vault opens
* `put` — Store a secret. The value comes from stdin (`printf … | cuora put cuora://ns/name`) or a hidden terminal prompt — never args, which land in shell history and `/proc`
* `get` — Print a secret's value to stdout — the escape hatch. Prefer `cuora run` so values never enter agent context; guardrails can deny this op
* `list` — List the refs stored in the selected env — names only, never values
* `rm` — Remove a secret from the selected env
* `rotate` — Rotate a secret to a new value (stdin or hidden prompt, like `put`); bumps version + rotated_at
* `run` — Run a command with declared secrets injected as env vars
* `env` — Print `export VAR='…'` lines for `eval "$(cuora env)"` — the human path (`run` is the agent path). Values print to stdout: `--json` emits a `VAR → value` map
* `check` — Validate config + the declared surface: `[envs]` routes point at declared vaults, vaults decrypt, every `[secrets]` ref resolves in its routed env. Exit 1 on findings
* `migrate` — Rewrite stored records for a wire/config upgrade. Currently one transform: `--private-refs` re-keys every plaintext-named row in each env routed to a cf vault with `[vaults.*] private_refs = true` — ciphertext moves verbatim, old keys are deleted after the new rows land
* `deploy` — Push a stored secret to a write-only deploy target (`[deploy.NAME]` in cuora.toml, e.g. a CF Secrets Store). The vault is the source of truth; the sink never gives the value back. With one configured target, `--target` may be omitted
* `serve` — Serve the Vault port over ndjson — one JSON request per stdin line, one response per stdout line, audit events on stderr unchanged. For orchestrators embedding cuora (peregrin); with `[serve.pdp]` configured, a policy decision point is consulted before every vault-touching op. `{"op":"manifest"}` on the wire describes the protocol
* `manifest` — Capabilities, JSON shapes, env vars, audit contract — agent self-discovery (always JSON)
* `schema` — JSON Schema for `cuora.toml`

###### **Options:**

* `--json` — Emit JSON — stable machine shapes on every verb; errors are `{"error": "…"}` on stderr with a non-zero exit
* `--env <ENV>` — Env context — `dev`/`staging`/`prod`/custom. Overrides `CUORA_ENV`; default `dev`
* `--config <PATH>` — Config file, overriding the search ($CUORA_CONFIG → ./cuora.toml → ~/.config/cuora/cuora.toml)
* `--actor <ACTOR>` — Actor attribution for audit events (default $CUORA_ACTOR, else $USER)

## `cuora init`

Bootstrap: store the age identity in the system keyring when a session secret store is reachable — importing an existing identity.txt rather than orphaning it — else the `~/.config/cuora/identity.txt` keyfile (0600). Verifies the vault opens

**Usage:** `cuora init [OPTIONS]`

###### **Options:**

* `--with-file` — Force the identity keyfile even when a keyring is available — the headless/CI mode

## `cuora put`

Store a secret. The value comes from stdin (`printf … | cuora put cuora://ns/name`) or a hidden terminal prompt — never args, which land in shell history and `/proc`

**Usage:** `cuora put <RREF>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<RREF>` — `cuora://` ref, e.g. cuora://billing/stripe

## `cuora get`

Print a secret's value to stdout — the escape hatch. Prefer `cuora run` so values never enter agent context; guardrails can deny this op

**Usage:** `cuora get <RREF>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<RREF>` — `cuora://` ref

## `cuora list`

List the refs stored in the selected env — names only, never values

**Usage:** `cuora list`

## `cuora rm`

Remove a secret from the selected env

**Usage:** `cuora rm <RREF>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<RREF>` — `cuora://` ref

## `cuora rotate`

Rotate a secret to a new value (stdin or hidden prompt, like `put`); bumps version + rotated_at

**Usage:** `cuora rotate <RREF>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<RREF>` — `cuora://` ref

## `cuora run`

Run a command with declared secrets injected as env vars.

Injection surface = `[secrets]` in cuora.toml plus `-s VAR=cuora://ref` ad-hoc pairs; nothing else is injectable. Two exec modes after `--`:

`cuora run -- 'pnpm test | tee log'` — one string → `bash -c`

`cuora run -- pnpm test --filter x` — argv → direct exec

argv mode needs no shell quoting — prefer it when the command has arguments. Exit code is the child's.

**Usage:** `cuora run [OPTIONS] -- <CMD>...`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<CMD>` — Command to run (after `--`). One arg → `bash -c`; several → `argv[0]` exec'd directly with the rest

###### **Options:**

* `-s`, `--secret <VAR=CUORA_REF>` — Extra `VAR=cuora://ref` pairs to inject (refused when `[guardrails] deny_adhoc` is set)

## `cuora env`

Print `export VAR='…'` lines for `eval "$(cuora env)"` — the human path (`run` is the agent path). Values print to stdout: `--json` emits a `VAR → value` map

**Usage:** `cuora env [OPTIONS]`

###### **Options:**

* `-s`, `--secret <VAR=CUORA_REF>` — Extra `VAR=cuora://ref` pairs to resolve

## `cuora check`

Validate config + the declared surface: `[envs]` routes point at declared vaults, vaults decrypt, every `[secrets]` ref resolves in its routed env. Exit 1 on findings

**Usage:** `cuora check`

## `cuora migrate`

Rewrite stored records for a wire/config upgrade. Currently one transform: `--private-refs` re-keys every plaintext-named row in each env routed to a cf vault with `[vaults.*] private_refs = true` — ciphertext moves verbatim, old keys are deleted after the new rows land

**Usage:** `cuora migrate [OPTIONS]`

###### **Options:**

* `--private-refs` — Re-key cf-vault rows under HMAC-derived storage keys, attaching the encrypted `name` blob (P-004)

## `cuora deploy`

Push a stored secret to a write-only deploy target (`[deploy.NAME]` in cuora.toml, e.g. a CF Secrets Store). The vault is the source of truth; the sink never gives the value back. With one configured target, `--target` may be omitted

**Usage:** `cuora deploy [OPTIONS] <RREF>`

###### **Arguments:**

* `<RREF>` — `cuora://` ref to push

###### **Options:**

* `--target <NAME>` — Deploy target name (`[deploy.NAME]`); required when several are configured

## `cuora serve`

Serve the Vault port over ndjson — one JSON request per stdin line, one response per stdout line, audit events on stderr unchanged. For orchestrators embedding cuora (peregrin); with `[serve.pdp]` configured, a policy decision point is consulted before every vault-touching op. `{"op":"manifest"}` on the wire describes the protocol

**Usage:** `cuora serve`

## `cuora manifest`

Capabilities, JSON shapes, env vars, audit contract — agent self-discovery (always JSON)

**Usage:** `cuora manifest`

## `cuora schema`

JSON Schema for `cuora.toml`

**Usage:** `cuora schema`

# Config — `cuora.toml`

## Top level

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vaults` | `{name: vault}` | optional | Named vault backends. `local` always exists implicitly (age, default paths); an entry only overrides it or adds more. |
| `envs` | `{env: vault|{vault}}` | optional | Env → vault routing. Envs not listed route to `local`; `dev`/`staging`/`prod` always exist. |
| `secrets` | `{VAR: cuora://ref}` | optional | The declared secret surface: env-var name → `cuora://` ref. Bounds what `run`/`env` may inject — least privilege, no ambient vault dump. |
| `deploy` | `{name: target}` | optional | Named deploy targets — write-only sinks (`cuora deploy` pushes a stored value in; nothing ever reads one back). |
| `guardrails` | `table` | optional | Advisory op guardrails — accident prevention for standalone use, honestly *not* a policy boundary (a locally claimed actor is spoofable by construction). |
| `serve` | `table` | optional | The `cuora serve` surface — ndjson request/response on stdio plus the optional policy decision point. Absent, serve runs with no PDP — same advisory posture as the single-shot CLI. |
| `identity` | `IdentityConfig` | optional | Which backend holds the age identity — `[identity]`. Absent → `keyring` (fail closed; `auto`/`file` opt out). |

## `[vaults.NAME]` — a named vault backend

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kind` | `string` | optional | Backend kind — `"age"` (built-in, local file) or `"cf"` (self-hosted Cloudflare Worker + D1, `cuora-vault-cf`). |
| `path` | `string` | optional | Vault file path override (age impl; `~` is *not* expanded — write the path in full). |
| `identity` | `string` | optional | Age identity file override (`CUORA_IDENTITY_FILE` wins over this; see `cuora-ops`). `cf` vaults decrypt with the same keyfile — all vault impls store age ciphertext (ADR-0001). |
| `recipients` | `list` | optional | Extra age recipients to encrypt to, beyond the identity's public key (`age1…` strings). |
| `url` | `string` | optional | Worker base URL (`cf` impl), e.g. `https://cuora-vault.you.workers.dev`. |
| `token_env` | `string` | optional | Name of the env var holding the bearer token (`cf` impl) — the token *name* lives in config, the token *value* only in the process env. |
| `tokens` | `BTreeMap<Env, Ref>` | optional | Per-env scoped credentials (`cf` impl, P-003): env → the `cuora://` ref of a token stored in the `local` vault. Each resolved token authenticates as `CuoraHmac &lt;ref-path&gt;, ts, nonce, sig` — the ref path is the wire `token_id`. Token *refs* live in config, never token values. |
| `private_refs` | `bool` | optional | Opt-in private ref metadata (`cf` impl, P-004): storage keys become HMAC-derived hex and every record carries an age-encrypted `name` blob, so the remote store can't see which secrets exist. Default false; `cuora migrate --private-refs` rewrites existing rows. |
| `cache` | `CacheScope` | optional | Read-through encrypted local cache in front of this vault (P-007): `true` caches every env; a name or list scopes it — `cache = "dev"` or `cache = ["dev", "staging"]`. Rows land at `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/cuora/&lt;name&gt;.age` as ordinary age ciphertext carrying the remote `version`/`rotated_at` verbatim; freshness is TTL-bounded (`cache_ttl_secs`) and writes are always remote-first. Meant for remote backends — `dev` may cache, `prod` should live-fetch. |
| `cache_ttl_secs` | `int` | optional | Cache freshness window in seconds — a cached row or env listing younger than this answers without a remote round-trip; past it the remote is re-fetched and the cache updated. A remote *failure* falls back to the stale copy — the offline mode. Absent → 300. |

## `[envs]` — env → vault routing (table form)

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vault` | `string` | required | Vault name in `[vaults]` (or the implicit `local`). |

## `[deploy.NAME]` — a write-only push target

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kind` | `string` | optional | Target kind — `"cf-secrets-store"` (Cloudflare account Secrets Store, `cuora-deploy-cf`). |
| `account_id` | `string` | optional | Cloudflare account id (`cf-secrets-store`). |
| `store_id` | `string` | optional | Secrets Store id (`cf-secrets-store`). |
| `token_env` | `string` | optional | Name of the env var holding the API token — never the token itself (`cf-secrets-store` defaults to `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`). |
| `base_url` | `string` | optional | API base URL override — for tests, gateways, and self-hosted proxies. Defaults to `https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4`. |

## `[guardrails]` — advisory op table

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `default` | `"allow"|"deny"` | optional | Fallback for ops in neither list. |
| `allow` | `op list` | optional | Ops always allowed. |
| `deny` | `op list` | optional | Ops always refused — deny wins over allow. |
| `deny_adhoc` | `bool` | optional | Refuse `-s VAR=cuora://ref` ad-hoc injection on `run`/`env` (MED-5). Without it, a posture like `deny = ["get"]` is sidestepped: `cuora run -s V=cuora://x -- printenv V` *is* a get. Declared `[secrets]` injection is unaffected — the declared surface is auditable config, not an ad-hoc grab. |

## `[serve]` — the `cuora serve` surface

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pdp` | `table` | optional | The external policy decision point serve consults before every op that can materialize (`get`/`put`/`rm`/`rotate`/ `list`/`check`). Absent, no consult happens — the advisory posture only. |

## `[serve.pdp]` — the external policy decision point

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `exec` | `string` | required | The exec driver command — run via `sh -c` once per decision, request JSON on stdin, verdict JSON on stdout. **Trust root**: the line authorizes shell exec; the child inherits only the `cuora-shell` env allowlist. `cuora serve` warns when this arrives via an implicit `./cuora.toml` — pin config with `--config`/`$CUORA_CONFIG`. |
| `allow_on_error` | `bool` | optional | What an unreachable PDP means. `false` (default) fails **closed** — the op is denied; a policy engine that can't answer must not silently mean "allowed". `true` fails open — the op runs anyway and the audit event records the degraded verdict. |
| `timeout_ms` | `int` | optional | Per-decision deadline in milliseconds — the child is killed and the consult counts as *unreachable* past it. A hung or flooding PDP must never freeze the serve loop; absent → 5000. |

## `[envs]` route forms

Either a bare vault name or the table above:

```toml
[envs]
dev = "local"
prod = { vault = "cloud" }
```

## Constraints

* `deny_unknown_fields`: typos in field names fail the load.
* Search order: `--config` → `$CUORA_CONFIG` → `./cuora.toml` →
  `~/.config/cuora/cuora.toml`. The file is optional — no
  `cuora.toml` anywhere just means defaults (local age vault,
  `dev` env).
* Token values never live in the file — `token_env` fields name
  the env var that carries them.
* `cuora schema` emits the JSON Schema for this shape;
  `cuora check` validates a real file end-to-end.

url: /cuora/reference/audit-events.md
---
# Audit events

The audit wire: one ndjson line on **stderr** per op outcome,
plus an OTLP span per event when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`
is set. cuora keeps no local ledger (ADR-0001 — aggregation is
peregrin's); the stderr stream *is* the human contract and the
OTLP stream the machine one, so a wrapper — peregrin, sepia,
your own harness — can capture either, and a human sees a
breadcrumb.

## Shape

```json
{"ts":"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z","actor":"devin","op":"run","rref":"billing/stripe","env":"dev","outcome":"ok"}
```

| field | notes |
| --- | --- |
| `ts` | RFC 3339, UTC |
| `actor` | `--actor` → `CUORA_ACTOR` → `$USER`/`$LOGNAME` → `anon`. Self-claimed — attribution, not identity |
| `op` | the verb: `init put get list rm rotate run env check deploy migrate serve manifest schema` |
| `rref` | the resolved ref path, env pin stripped — same on `denied`/`error` when the arg parses, else the raw arg verbatim. **Absent** on op-scoped events |
| `env` | the env the op ran under |
| `outcome` | `ok` | `denied` | `error` |
| `policy` | **serve-path only, optional** — the PDP verdict `{allow, reason?, obligations?}` behind the outcome; absent on every other path |

## When events fire

| event | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ok`, ref-scoped | one **per ref** materialized or mutated — `put`, `get`, `rotate`, `rm`, `deploy`, `migrate` (per rewritten ref), and per resolved ref inside `run`/`env` |
| `ok`, op-scoped | ref-less verb completed — `init`, `list`, `check`, `migrate`, `serve` |
| `denied` | `[guardrails]` — or a serve-path PDP verdict of `allow: false` (including fail-closed on an unreachable PDP) — refused the op before it touched the vault; `rref` is the requested ref (normalized when parseable) |
| `error` | the op ran and failed — missing secret, vault i/o, bad ref; a `check` with findings also audits `error` (it exits 1); also emitted when config load itself fails (best-effort actor/env from flags + process env) |

Two deliberate silences:

* `manifest`, `schema`, `gen-cli-docs` run before config load —
  pure introspection, no event.
* A `run` child's non-zero exit is the *child's* outcome — no
  `error` event for it. cuora's own exit code is the child's.

## `serve` and the `policy` field

`cuora serve` emits the same events — `get`/`put`/`rm`/`rotate`
requests audit exactly like the CLI verbs, under the request's
claimed `actor` when it carries one. The PDP consult covers the
ops that can materialize — `get`/`put`/`rm`/`rotate` *and*
`list`/`check` (record decrypts, vault probes, scoped-token
gets) — so a `check`'s incidental token `get`s ride the same
`policy`-bearing events. On the serve path only, every event a
consulted `[serve.pdp]` gated gains a `policy` object —
`{allow, reason?, obligations?}` — so the stream shows the
verdict behind the outcome: a PDP allow, a PDP deny
(`outcome: "denied"`, `policy.allow: false`), or a degraded
allow recorded when `allow_on_error` overrode an unreachable
PDP. The `serve` verb itself closes with one op-scoped `ok`.
See [the serve protocol](serve-protocol.md).

## OTLP export

Set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` (e.g. `http://localhost:4318`)
and every audit event is additionally buffered as an
`cuora.<op>` span — `ExportTraceServiceRequest` JSON posted to
`<endpoint>/v1/traces` on flush. Span attributes mirror the
ndjson fields: `cuora.op`, `cuora.rref` (when present), `cuora.env`,
`cuora.actor`, `cuora.outcome`, and `cuora.policy.*` on serve-path
events; `Outcome::Error` marks the span `STATUS_CODE_ERROR`.
`service.name` comes from `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` (default `cuora`).

Flush timing: CLI verbs export once at exit; `cuora serve` flushes
per request (it's long-running).

Related env vars: `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` (`k=v` pairs,
percent-decoded), `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` (ms, default
10000\), `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true` turns export off entirely, and
`CUORA_AUDIT_STDERR=0` silences the stderr wire (OTLP-only mode).

## Failure posture

Audit emission is best-effort on both wires: a closed stderr
(broken pipe) never takes the broker down — the write error is
swallowed by design — and a failed OTLP export warns once on
stderr, never fails the op.

Note: stderr can also carry non-ndjson `cuora:` *notice* lines
(permission warnings, keyring fallback notes) — UX chatter, not
audit wire. Consumers parsing stderr as pure ndjson should
tolerate lines that don't start with `{`.

## Granularity

Per-ref events fire when a value crosses the store boundary
toward a caller: `get`, `put`, `rotate`, `rm`, `deploy`, `run`,
`env`, `migrate` (per rewritten ref), and serve
`get`/`put`/`rotate`/`rm`. Bulk reads —
`list`, `check`, serve `list` — emit **op-scoped** events
only: they decrypt records internally to verify or enumerate, but
no value is returned to the caller, so there is no per-ref
materialization to attribute. If your threat model counts
"decrypted in-process" as materialization, treat bulk ops as
single events covering N refs — the op name tells you which verb
ran, not which refs it touched.

url: /cuora/reference/serve-protocol.md
---
# The `cuora serve` protocol

`cuora serve` is the Vault port over newline-delimited JSON — the
surface orchestrators (peregrin) embed. One JSON request per
**stdin** line, one JSON response per **stdout** line, and the
[audit wire](audit-events.md) stays on **stderr**, unchanged —
three separate fds, so a reply never rides the event stream and
an event never answers a request. Protocol version:
`cuora-serve/1` — send `{"op":"manifest"}` on the wire for the
machine-readable self-description.

Serve is a thin front over the same `cuora-ops` plumbing the CLI
uses: `[envs]` routing, `cuora://<env>/…` pins, and audit events
are identical. `run`/`env`/`deploy`/`init`/`migrate`/`schema`/
`gen-cli-docs` stay single-shot CLI verbs — serve covers what an
embedder needs in-process.

## Requests

```json
{"id": 1, "op": "get", "ref": "cuora://billing/stripe",
 "env": "prod", "actor": "agent:peregrin", "attestation": "…"}
```

| field | notes |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | any JSON value — echoed verbatim (absent → `null`), ≤ 4 KiB serialized |
| `op` | `get` | `put` | `rm` | `rotate` | `list` | `check` | `manifest` | `shutdown` |
| `ref` | `cuora://ns/name` ≤ 1 KiB — required by the four vault ops; an `cuora://<env>/…` pin overrides `env` |
| `env` | per-request env override — else the loaded context (`--env`/`CUORA_ENV`) |
| `value` | plaintext ≤ 64 KiB — required by `put`/`rotate`. Values cross this wire deliberately: the parent owns the channel exactly like it owns `cuora get`'s stdout |
| `actor` | claimed actor id ≤ 256 B — advisory attribution recorded on audit events; validated, never verified |
| `attestation` | opaque identity claim ≤ 64 KiB — passed to the PDP verbatim, never interpreted by cuora |

Hard bounds on the wire: a request line may be at most **4 MiB**
— an oversized line answers `bad_request` and the reader resyncs
to the next line, so a broken embedder can't exhaust memory.
Blank or whitespace-only lines get **no reply** — legal
keep-alive, unanswered. A non-UTF-8 line is a `bad_request`, not
a crash.

## Responses

```json
{"id": 1, "ok": true, "result": {"ref": "cuora://billing/stripe", "env": "prod",
 "value": "…", "version": 3, "created_at": "…", "rotated_at": "…"},
 "policy": {"allow": true, "reason": "…", "obligations": ["…"]}}
```

```json
{"id": 2, "ok": false, "error": {"code": "denied", "message": "denied by policy: no prod reads"}}
```

`policy` appears on a response whenever a PDP was consulted for
that op — the same verdict the audit event records.

| error code | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `bad_request` | malformed/oversized/non-UTF-8 line, missing `ref`/`value`, invalid ref/env/actor, field over cap — the loop keeps serving |
| `unknown_op` | op not in the table (a real CLI verb reports "not served — use the single-shot CLI") |
| `denied` | `[guardrails]` or PDP refusal |
| `pdp_unreachable` | the PDP couldn't answer (spawn, non-zero exit, timeout, flooded/oversized/unparseable verdict) and `allow_on_error` is false — fail-closed |
| `not_found` | the ref isn't stored in that env |
| `op_error` | vault/config/io failure |

`shutdown` replies then exits cleanly; EOF on stdin exits too.
`manifest` and `shutdown` are protocol meta-ops: they skip
guardrails and the PDP consult by design — gating session
lifecycle is the embedder's spawn decision, not a
materialization.

## The policy decision point — `[serve.pdp]`

Configured, serve consults the PDP **before every op that can
materialize** — `get`/`put`/`rm`/`rotate`, and `list`/`check`
too: `list` decrypts every record's metadata and `check` probes
vaults, including scoped-token `get`s and outbound signed HTTP
against cf vaults. Nothing crosses the vault boundary without a
verdict. `manifest`/`shutdown` are meta-ops and don't consult.
`[guardrails]` still apply on the serve path (the advisory
layer, checked before the consult), and request validation runs
before the consult too — a doomed request never spawns a PDP.

```toml
[serve.pdp]
exec = "peregrin policy decide"   # sh -c per decision
allow_on_error = false            # default: fail closed
timeout_ms = 5000                 # default: 5s per consult
```

A `[serve.pdp] exec` line is **trust-root config**: it
authorizes shell execution. When `cuora serve` loads it from an
*implicit* `./cuora.toml` (the search path, not a pinned
`--config`/`$CUORA_CONFIG` or `~/.config/cuora/`), it warns on
stderr — the working directory decides what code runs.

The `exec` command runs once per decision — request JSON on
stdin, verdict JSON on stdout, stderr discarded. The child
inherits only the `cuora-shell` env allowlist (same scrub
`cuora run` applies): `CUORA_CF_TOKEN`, `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`,
and every other parent credential stay out of the decider.

```json
{"actor": "agent:peregrin", "attestation": "…", "op": "get",
 "env": "prod", "ref": "billing/stripe"}
```

`ref` is the resolved path with the env pin stripped — and is
**absent** on `list`/`check` consults, which carry no ref.

```json
{"allow": true, "reason": "…", "obligations": ["redact", "session-bound"]}
```

`allow` is required; `reason` and `obligations` are free-form
context the PDP wants on record (allow-with-conditions — cuora
records them; enforcing them is the requester's job). A deny is
a `denied` response plus a `denied` audit event — no vault
access.

A consult is hard-bounded so a misbehaving PDP can't take the
broker with it: the child is killed at `timeout_ms`, the verdict
is capped at 64 KiB (a flooding child blocks on its own pipe and
dies on the deadline — it cannot sink memory), and the request
write can't deadlock against a child that never reads stdin.

Spawn failure, non-zero exit, timeout, an oversized or
unparseable verdict is **unreachable** → the op is denied
(`pdp_unreachable`) unless `allow_on_error = true`, which runs
the op anyway and records the degraded verdict (`policy.reason`
says why). Fail-closed is the default because an unanswered
policy engine must not silently mean "allowed".

Why `exec` and not a socket or HTTP: zero new dependencies, sync
only, no daemon lifecycle. A PDP that wants a persistent
endpoint can put `socat`/`nc`/`curl` in its own exec line — the
wire stays the same. Note the per-op cost: every consult spawns
a fresh `sh -c`, `list` decrypts each record, and `check` probes
every vault — batch reads rather than looping `list`.

## Actor claims are advisory

`actor` and `attestation` are *claims*, not proof — cuora
validates the actor string's shape and passes both through to
audit and the PDP. Signed, short-lived attestation is the PDP's
side (peregrin's design, a later decision); ADR-0003 only fixes
the pass-through seam.

url: /cuora/reference/env-vars.md
---
# Environment variables

Process env vars cuora itself reads. (The vars in `[secrets]` are
yours — this is cuora's own surface; `cuora manifest` reports the
same table.)

| var | default | used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CUORA_CONFIG` | — | config file override, between `--config` and `./cuora.toml` in the search order |
| `CUORA_ENV` | `dev` | env context — resolution + routing (`--env` wins) |
| `CUORA_ACTOR` | `$USER` → `anon` | audit attribution (`--actor` wins). Self-claimed |
| `CUORA_IDENTITY_FILE` | `~/.config/cuora/identity.txt` | age identity keyfile for every vault impl — pins file mode outright |
| `CUORA_IDENTITY_BACKEND` | `keyring` | `keyring` (default — fail closed, no file fallback) | `auto` (keyring → keyfile fallback, for headless) | `file` (never probe the keyring); wins over `[identity] backend` |
| `CUORA_CF_TOKEN` | — | bearer token for `kind = "cf"` vaults — *default* name; `[vaults.*].token_env` picks another |
| `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` | — | API token for `cf-secrets-store` deploy sinks — *default* name; `[deploy.*].token_env` picks another |
| `CUORA_AUDIT_STDERR` | on | `0`/`false`/`off`/`no` silences the stderr ndjson audit wire — OTLP-only mode |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | — | OTLP/HTTP collector base — audit events export as `cuora.<op>` spans to `<endpoint>/v1/traces`; `http://` is accepted only for loopback collectors (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`) — same policy as cf vault URLs |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` | — | `k=v,k2=v2` auth headers for the OTLP endpoint (values percent-decoded) |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` | `10000` | export timeout in ms |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `cuora` | `service.name` resource attribute on exported spans |
| `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED` | — | `true`/`1` disables OTLP export entirely |

Honored XDG paths (when the matching override is unset):

| var | falls back to |
| --- | --- |
| `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | `~/.config` — identity + user-level `cuora.toml` |
| `XDG_DATA_HOME` | `~/.local/share` — the default `vault.age` |

Two rules of thumb:

* `token_env` config fields name env vars — the token *value*
  only ever lives in the process env.
* `CUORA_ACTOR` is a self-claimed string for the audit trail, not
  authentication; see the [threat model](../explanation/threat-model.md).

# Architecture

Ports-and-adapters over a flat `crates/` workspace. `cuora-core`
is pure domain — `cuora://` refs, the redacting `Secret` newtype,
the env axis, actor attribution — with no I/O. Ports are traits
(`cuora-config`, `cuora-vault`, `cuora-deploy`); impls live in
separate crates; `crates/cuora-cli` (package `cuora`) is the
composition root that wires impls to verbs.

Design rules:

* **No `unsafe`, no async** — the binary stays dependency-light
  and synchronous; vault impls that speak HTTP use a blocking
  client (`ureq`), so no runtime embeds anywhere.
* **`Secret` never exposes plaintext** — no `Display`/`Debug` of
  the value; `.expose()` is the only way out, called at edges
  only (child env injection, `cuora env` exports, `get`).
* **Stores hold ciphertext only** — every vault impl encrypts
  client-side with age (ADR-0001); a remote vault is ciphertext
  over the wire *and* at rest, never a plaintext service.
* **Ports are conformance-tested** — `cuora-testkit` runs the same
  contract suite against every vault impl (`cuora-vault-age`,
  `cuora-vault-cf`): upsert/rotate/list/env-isolation semantics
  can't drift per backend.
* **One ops shell** — `cuora-ops` owns config load, env→vault
  routing, the env-pin rule, and audit emission; the CLI and
  `cuora serve` are both thin front-ends over it and cannot
  diverge.

| crate | layer | purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `cuora-core` | domain | cuora domain core: cuora:// refs, redacting Secret, env axis, actor, config model — pure, no I/O |
| `cuora-config` | port | Config port: where cuora.toml-shaped config comes from |
| `cuora-deploy` | port | Deploy port: write-only push targets (sinks) for secret values — never a source |
| `cuora-vault` | port | Vault port: readable secret stores — get/put/rm/list/rotate, per-env; every impl stores opaque ciphertext |
| `cuora-ops` | ops | cuora ops I/O: config load, env/ref resolution, vault open, verb plumbing, audit emission |
| `cuora` | engine | cuora — secrets broker for agents: reference URIs, redaction, env-injection CLI |
| `cuora-config-toml` | adapter | Config impl: cuora.toml file (explicit path, env, ./, ~/.config) |
| `cuora-deploy-cf` | adapter | Deploy impl: push secret values to a Cloudflare account Secrets Store (write-only sink) via the CF API v4 |
| `cuora-driver` | adapter | tamias-driver-cuora — pavo view driver over cuora vault metadata (read-only; never renders secret values) plus engine ops dispatching to the cuora lib |
| `cuora-identity` | adapter | Identity port: where the age identity (master key) comes from — file, keyring, later sealed variants |
| `cuora-identity-file` | adapter | Identity impl: the ~/.config/cuora/identity.txt age keyfile (0600) — the explicit file backend (headless/CI opt-out) |
| `cuora-identity-keyring` | adapter | Identity impl: the platform session secret store (secret-service / Keychain / Credential Manager) via keyring-core |
| `cuora-notice` | adapter | Process-wide UX notices — cuora:-prefixed stderr notes, mutable for terminal-owning surfaces |
| `cuora-serve` | adapter | cuora serve — the ndjson request/response IPC surface orchestrators embed, with the external policy-decision consult (P-005) |
| `cuora-shell` | adapter | Run a command in a working directory via bash -c — the generic shell-out helper |
| `cuora-testkit` | adapter | Vault conformance suite — every cuora-vault impl passes the same contract tests (fake values only) |
| `cuora-vault-age` | adapter | Local vault impl: one age-x25519-encrypted JSON doc — the v1 default backend |
| `cuora-vault-cached` | adapter | Composite vault impl: read-through age-encrypted local cache in front of any backend (P-007) |
| `cuora-vault-cf` | adapter | Remote vault impl: self-hosted Cloudflare Worker + D1 holding per-secret age ciphertext — the Worker never sees plaintext |

## Front-ends

* **`cuora` (CLI)** — clap verbs + `--json`/`manifest`/`schema` for
  machines; the agent interface. There is no standalone binary:
  the command ships as the `libraries/cuora` tamias pack — a
  generated `bins[]` shim → `tamias-driver-cuora`'s `cli`
  passthrough → `cuora::run_from`.
* **`tamias-driver-cuora`** — the pavo view driver: read-only
  vault *metadata* (never renders values), plus the engine ops
  surface (`ops`/`run`/`cli.*` wire queries) that backs the shim.
* **`cuora serve`** — ndjson IPC over the Vault port with an
  exec-driven `[serve.pdp]` policy-decision hook (ADR-0003);
  peregrin's embedding point.

## Boundary — secret materialization only

cuora owns refs, vaults, env injection, redaction, and the audit
wire. Neighbors own theirs — see
[boundaries](boundaries.md) for the full map.

---

---
url: /cuora/explanation/threat-model.md
---
# Threat model

What cuora protects against, honestly — and what it explicitly
does not.

## Protects against

* **Plaintext in the repo** — code and config carry `cuora://`
  refs, never values. There is nothing to leak in a commit, a
  diff, a paste, or a prompt context.
* **Plaintext in shell history / process listings** — values
  never enter via CLI arguments (args land in `~/.bash_history`
  and `/proc/*/cmdline`). `put`/`rotate` read stdin or a hidden
  `/dev/tty` prompt.
* **Plaintext in agent context** — `cuora run` injects values into
  the child's environment; the agent that spawned it sees the
  child's *output*, never the variable. `[secrets]` bounds the
  injectable surface so a `run` can't dump the whole vault.
* **Accidental printing** — `Secret` has no `Display`/`Debug` of
  the value (`.expose()` only), `list` is names + metadata only,
  and `tamias-driver-cuora`'s pavo view is metadata-only by
  construction — it never renders secret values.
* **Ciphertext at rest, everywhere** — every vault impl stores
  age ciphertext. The local file is unreadable without the
  identity; the `cf` remote store holds ciphertext over the wire
  *and* in D1 — a compromised worker yields blobs, not values.
  With `[vaults.*] private_refs = true` it can't even see *which*
  secrets exist: storage keys are HMAC-derived hex and the real
  ref travels in an age-encrypted `name` blob.
* **Token leakage on the cf wire** — scoped tokens
  (`CUORA_VAULT_TOKENS`) bound a leaked credential to its
  `{env, read, write}` scope instead of every env forever, and
  CuoraHmac request signing means the token never travels at all
  (a ±60s window bounds replay). All auth compares are
  constant-time.
* **Silent misuse** — every materialization, denial, and error
  emits an ndjson audit event on stderr, so capture is a wrapper
  away. `check` fails closed on a vault that won't decrypt, and
  on a mixed-mode cf vault (private config + plaintext rows).

## Does NOT protect against

* **A determined local actor** — `CUORA_ACTOR` is self-claimed
  (attribution, not identity) and `[guardrails]` are advisory:
  anyone who can edit `cuora.toml` or run the binary can bypass
  them. They prevent *accidents*, not adversaries. Real
  multi-actor policy and enforcement belong to **peregrin**.
* **The identity's host protection** — the master key lives in
  the session keyring by default (ADR-0002), which protects it
  about as well as your login session — and the default backend
  fails closed rather than silently downgrading. The `0600`
  keyfile (`identity.txt`, raw key material like an unencrypted
  SSH key) is reached only via explicit opt-in: `backend =
  "auto"`/`"file"`, `CUORA_IDENTITY_FILE`, or `[vaults.*].identity`
  — the headless/CI path, where no session store exists anyway.
  Either way, UID-level compromise reaches it: the keyring
  raises the bar, it is not a TPM.
* **The child process** — once `run` injects env vars, the child
  owns them (`/proc/<pid>/environ`, core dumps, the child logging
  its own env). cuora's guarantee ends at `exec`.
* **Deploy sinks** — `cuora deploy` pushes plaintext into the sink
  by design (CF Secrets Store is write-only); a sink compromise
  is outside cuora's boundary — it crosses exactly once, at push.
* **Access patterns** — `private_refs` hides *which* secrets
  exist, not *when* they're touched: request timing and row
  counts are still observable to the store. Oblivious access is
  out of scope.
* **Host compromise in general** — an attacker who can read your
  memory, ptrace the broker, or impersonate your UID already won;
  cuora raises the bar for *accidental* and *casual* leaks, not
  root.

## In one line

cuora makes the *default* posture "values never appear in repos,
prompts, args, logs, or agent context" — and records every time
one still crosses.

---

---
url: /cuora/explanation/boundaries.md
---
# Boundaries

cuora is one organism in a stack — it owns **secret
materialization** and nothing else. If a feature needs another
kind of memory or authority, it belongs to a neighbor.

| neighbor | owns | how it meets cuora |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **myco** | work memory — tasks, issues, proposals, plans, ADRs, handoffs | this repo's `project/` ledger is myco's; cuora has no PM surface |
| **sturn** | ephemeral coordination — live claims/ops/topics | not secrets: sturn state is transient, cuora state is sealed |
| **kuda** | code memory — symbol/index knowledge | cuora refs name *secrets*, not code entities |
| **peregrin** | orchestration — campaigns, multi-actor arbitration, policy | campaigns consume secrets via `cuora run`; audit aggregation + real policy are peregrin's (`CUORA_ACTOR` is self-claimed inside cuora); `cuora serve` — the ndjson IPC wire + `[serve.pdp]` exec consult (ADR-0003) — is its embedding point |
| **bupha / ci-gate** | CI gate | bupha is the CI repo — the org gate is the peregrin `ci-gate` campaign, mid-migration back to bupha (`type: bupha` bundles); it asserted no plaintext secrets land in pipelines, `cuora check` in pipeline steps |
| **mimus** | critic | secrets resolve env → cuora → legacy (keyring, `~/.config/mimus/env`) via `mimus-cuora` shelling `cuora`; vaults are canonical, writes land in them |
| **sepia** | session lifecycle | session wrappers can capture cuora's stderr audit stream |

## What that means in practice

* **A hosted vault service is in scope** — `cuora-vault-cf` is a
  store impl behind the same port, ciphertext-only, self-hosted.
* **A daemon is out of scope** — persistent coordination,
  multi-machine views, arbitration between actors → peregrin.
  cuora stays a sync, embeddable binary: env vars are the
  interface, no SDK.
* **Policy is out of scope** — `[guardrails]` are advisory
  accident prevention. Enforcement, identity, and unforgeable
  attribution are orchestration concerns.
* **The audit wire stops at stderr** — emitting ndjson is cuora's;
  collecting, storing, and alerting on it is peregrin's
  (ADR-0001 deliberately removed the local `audit.jsonl`).

---

---
url: /cuora/explanation/crypto-model.md
---
# Crypto model

One crypto choice everywhere, made once in ADR-0001: **age**.
Every vault impl stores age ciphertext; the same identity
unlocks the local file vault and the remote `cf` vault alike.

## The pieces

* **Identity** — one X25519 keypair, held by an `cuora-identity`
  impl (ADR-0002): the **session keyring** (secret-service,
  macOS Keychain, Credential Manager) by default — fail closed —
  or the `~/.config/cuora/identity.txt` keyfile (mode `0600`)
  under `auto`/`file` modes or an explicit pin. An explicit
  file — `CUORA_IDENTITY_FILE` or `[vaults.*].identity` — pins the
  keyfile outright; that is the headless/CI path. `[identity]
  backend` (or `CUORA_IDENTITY_BACKEND`) selects the mode:
  `keyring` (default) fails closed — no reachable store or
  stored identity is an error, the keyfile is never read;
  `auto` is the fallback described above — convenient on
  headless/CI, but a *silent* downgrade if a desktop session
  loses its store, so it's opt-in; `file` skips the store
  probe entirely. `cuora init`
  bootstraps whichever backend applies and prints the public
  `age1…` recipient. On a reachable-but-empty Secret Service (fresh
  daemon, no collections yet) the keyring impl claims the `default`
  collection alias on first use — `dbus-secret-service-keyring-store`'s
  create path can't bootstrap one itself (I-006).
* **Recipients** — `[vaults.*].recipients` encrypts to extra
  public keys beyond the identity's own — a team recipient list
  without sharing the private key.
* **Ciphertext at rest** — the local vault is a single
  age-encrypted file (`vault.age`); the `cf` vault stores
  per-secret age ciphertext in D1. Neither store — local disk,
  remote worker — holds plaintext or key material.
* **Seal/open at the edge** — values are plaintext only inside
  the cuora process, and only for as long as the op needs them.
  `Secret` is a `Zeroizing` newtype: memory is scrubbed on drop,
  and nothing but `.expose()` reads it.
* **HMAC alongside age** — the `cf` wire uses HMAC-SHA256 twice
  (P-003, P-004), keyed but unkeyed-payload, complementary to the
  age envelope: request *signing* so tokens never travel, and
  `ref_key` *derivation* so storage keys are unlinkable. Neither
  is a second encryption primitive — it's authentication and
  deterministic naming.

## Why age (and not KMS / libsodium / SSH keys)

* **One identity, every backend** — a remote vault that stores
  client-side ciphertext needs an offline asymmetric primitive;
  age gives recipient-style encryption with no service to trust.
* **Dependency posture** — the `age` crate (rage's Rust impl) is
  pulled with `default-features = false`: binary ciphertext, sync
  API, no async/armor/plugin machinery — the binary stays light
  per the workspace rules.
* **Interop for free** — the vault file decrypts with stock
  `rage`/`age` tooling, so a human is never locked into the CLI
  for disaster recovery.

## The cf wire (`cuora-vault-cf/2`)

* **Request signing** — `Authorization: CuoraHmac &lt;token_id&gt;, &lt;ts&gt;,
  &lt;sig&gt;` with `sig = hex HMAC-SHA256(token, method+path+ts+
  sha256hex(body))`. The token is the HMAC key and never crosses
  the wire; a ±60s timestamp window bounds replay. Worker-side,
  `CUORA_VAULT_TOKENS` maps `token_id → {env → {read, write}}`
  scopes — per-env credentials instead of one static bearer
  (which stays accepted during migration).
* **Private refs** — with `[vaults.*] private_refs = true`, the
  storage key is `ref_key = hex HMAC-SHA256(k, env + "/" + ref)`
  where `k = HMAC-SHA256(identity, "cuora-cf/private-refs/v1")`.
  Derivation is deterministic (lookup is a plain keyed read) and
  identity-bound (rotating the identity re-keys everything, via
  `cuora migrate --private-refs`). The real ref travels inside a
  `name` blob — age ciphertext — so `list` maps keys back while
  the store sees only hex.
* **Constant-time compares** — every token/signature comparison
  on the worker is a byte-wise XOR-fold over the longer input
  with length folded in; no early exit, no prefix oracle.

## What is deliberately not here

* **No KMS port yet** — managed-key backends (AWS KMS/Secrets
  Manager) were explored in the `cuora-vault-aws` spike to prove
  the `Vault` port generalizes to non-age stores; a KMS-backed
  *crypto* port is a later ADR, not v1.
* **No passphrase-wrapped identity file** — when the keyring is
  unavailable the keyfile is still raw age key material at
  `0600`, like an unencrypted SSH key. A passphrase-wrapped arm
  of the identity port is a later impl, not a new port.
* **No signing / integrity metadata** beyond what age's AEAD
  gives — tampered ciphertext fails decryption loudly, which is
  the correct failure.

url: /cuora/explanation/worktree-model.md
---
# The worktree model

Why `project/` and `docs/` live as git worktrees of orphan
branches inside this repo — and what that buys.

## The shape

```text
cuora/
├── crates/ …           ← code branch (main)
├── project/            ← worktree of the orphan `project` branch
│   ├── TODO.md  BACKLOG.md  index.md  meta.toml
│   └── issues/  proposals/  plans/  adrs/  handoffs/
├── docs/               ← worktree of the orphan `docs` branch
│   └── this site — VitePress sources
└── .gitignore          ← ignores project/ and docs/
```

Both worktrees share the repo's `.git` object store but have
histories disjoint from `main` — orphan roots, no code
ancestors. To tools they're ordinary directories; to
`git worktree list` they're checkouts of their own branches.

## Why orphan branches

Non-code state moves at its own cadence. On orphan branches,
ledger and docs commits never touch the code history: no
`chore: handoff T-009` noise in `main`'s log, no PM or docs-site
diffs in code PRs. Both dirs are gitignored on `main` — the
worktrees physically can't leak into a code commit.

## Why worktrees (not just branches)

The content has to be *visible* — agents read `project/`, humans
edit `docs/` — without `git checkout` swapping the code tree.
Worktrees keep all three branches checked out at once.

## `project/` — the PM ledger

Owned by **myco**, not cuora: this repo dogfoods the stack's PM
tool. The `project` branch history is the audit trail — every
mutating `myco` verb is one atomic commit. `myco init` created
the branch and worktree; agents go through `myco` verbs rather
than hand-editing when a verb exists.

## `docs/` — this site

The `docs` branch holds the VitePress + Diátaxis sources;
generated pages (`reference/cli.md`, `reference/config.md`, the
crate map in `architecture.md`, `reference/crate-api.md`) are
rebuilt by `docs/gen-*.py` and `cuora gen-cli-docs` — never
hand-edited. `cargo xtask site` builds the site; pushes deploy to
GitHub Pages at `9aia.com/cuora` via `scripts/deploy-docs.sh`.

See [architecture](architecture.md) for the crates the code side
is made of.

---

---
url: /cuora/getting-started.md
---
# Getting started

Install the `cuora` CLI, seal your first secret in the local
age-encrypted vault, and run a command that uses it — without the
value ever touching your terminal, a file, or an agent's context.

## Install

The `cuora` command ships as a tamias pack (`libraries/cuora`) — a
generated `bins[]` shim over `tamias-driver-cuora`, not a
cargo-installed binary. With `tamias` installed:

```sh
tamias install 9aia:cuora@0.2.0    # from the org registry
                                     # (private registry: set TAMIAS_REGISTRY_TOKEN)
```

From a checkout of this repo:

```sh
cargo xtask pack                            # stage the driver payload
tamias install --allow-drivers ./libraries/cuora   # deploys `cuora`
```

`cargo xtask install` additionally puts `tamias-driver-cuora`
itself on `PATH` (`~/.cargo/bin`).

## Bootstrap

```sh
cuora init
```

`init` stores your age identity where it's safest available and
verifies the vault at `~/.local/share/cuora/vault.age` opens. It's
idempotent — run it any time.

On a desktop session (GNOME Keyring, KeePassXC, KDE Wallet, macOS
Keychain, Windows Credential Manager) the identity lands in the
session keyring — it unlocks with login, no prompt. The default
backend is `keyring`: **fail closed** — if no session store is
reachable, `init` (and every other verb) errors rather than
silently downgrading to a file. Headless boxes (servers, CI,
containers, plain SSH) have no session bus, so there you opt out
explicitly — `[identity] backend = "auto"` in `cuora.toml` (probe
the keyring, fall back to the keyfile with a note), `"file"`
(never probe), or the `CUORA_IDENTITY_BACKEND` env var. The
fallback writes `~/.config/cuora/identity.txt` (mode `0600`) —
raw age key material, protect it like a private SSH key.
`cuora init --with-file` forces the keyfile; pinning
`CUORA_IDENTITY_FILE` or `[vaults.*].identity` in config does the
same — that's the deliberate headless/CI path.

Already have an `identity.txt`? `cuora init` imports it into the
keyring rather than orphaning it, and leaves the file as a backup
you can delete when ready. (On a brand-new keyring with no
collections yet, cuora claims the `default` collection alias
automatically — no manual step.)

## Seal a secret

Values never enter via CLI arguments — they would land in shell
history and `/proc`. Pipe them instead:

```sh
printf '%s' "$STRIPE_KEY" | cuora put cuora://billing/stripe
```

Interactive humans get a hidden `/dev/tty` prompt instead of
stdin. The value is encrypted to your identity and stored under
the `dev` env (the default context).

## Declare the surface

`[secrets]` in `cuora.toml` bounds what `run`/`env` may inject —
least privilege, no ambient vault dump:

```toml
[secrets]
STRIPE_KEY = "cuora://billing/stripe"
```

Config search: `./cuora.toml` → `~/.config/cuora/cuora.toml`
(`--config`/`$CUORA_CONFIG` override). No file at all is fine —
defaults are the local vault and the `dev` env.

## Run with secrets

```sh
cuora run -- 'curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $STRIPE_KEY" \
    https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges'
```

`run` resolves the declared refs, injects them as env vars into
the child only, and exits with the child's code. One arg after
`--` runs via `bash -c` (shell syntax, as above); several args
exec `argv[0]` directly with no shell. The value lives only in
that process — agents never see it.

## Check the setup

```sh
cuora check
```

Validates the config, that the routed vaults decrypt, and that
every `[secrets]` ref resolves — exit `1` on findings.

## Agent self-discovery

```sh
cuora manifest          # verbs, JSON shapes, env vars, audit contract (JSON)
cuora schema            # JSON Schema for cuora.toml
cuora <verb> --help     # every verb, self-documenting
```

`--json` is honored on every verb; errors are `{"error": "…"}`
on stderr with a non-zero exit. The
[cuora skill](https://github.com/9aia/cuora/tree/main/.agents/skills/cuora)
teaches agents the verbs.

## Where next

* [Your first secret](tutorials/first-secret.md) — a guided
  end-to-end in a throwaway HOME.

  modes, ad-hoc `-s` pairs, the `eval "$(cuora env)"` human path.
* [The threat model](explanation/threat-model.md) — what cuora
  does and does not protect against.
